name: Lena Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a normal shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43, new enough at the contact centre that I still need help with difficult payment claims. I finished secondary school and answer calls and chats at the junior desk. I sometimes use the approved suggestion tool after an experienced agent shows me where it works. I like when a caller can go away knowing who will fix the bill.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What happens when you go home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband works in school maintenance. We have a mortgage and two children, nine and twelve, so both wages matter. My pay is low here, less than a month's expenses are saved, and there are few similar jobs close enough to travel to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the quick reply button is helpful on ordinary delivery questions if someone checks it. The caller with a missing payment still needs an answer from a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm relieved the centre stays open, but I'm still the junior agent who asks for help on hard claims. Our mortgage leaves less than a month of bills saved, and my husband's maintenance wages cannot carry four of us alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep answering assigned calls and use the approved suggestion tool only on the questions my trainer has checked. From this payday through the first year, we'll stop the children's extra streaming package and put that amount in our household reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The software isn't the main worry in this picture; the thin cushion is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the household rely on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My husband fixes things at the school, and his hours are regular for now. Our children are nine and twelve, so a change in my pay would still show up at the dinner table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When do you use the suggestion tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I only use the suggestion tool after another agent shows me a reliable answer. If the account note is unclear, I call the trainer rather than send the suggested line.

I'd keep a **person** on missing-payment calls.
think: I still fear a **pay gap** because our mortgage and savings leave little room.
do: Keep taking **assigned calls** and asking my trainer about hard claims.
Cancel the **extra streaming package** this payday.
Save the **cancelled cost** in our household reserve each payday.

fieldNote: Her **mortgage pressure** persists under a mild AI scenario.

Save the cancelled package cost each payday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the supervisor to show which jobs remain once the easy calls go to software. A junior agent cannot learn difficult claims if there is no paid time left to practise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could lose hours before I get good at this job. There are few other centres near us, and a mortgage means I cannot treat a training promise as pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask to practise two disputed claims a week with my trainer during paid shifts and log errors from the approved suggestion tool. If my hours shrink in the first year, I'll ask the nearby care home whether it has a posted paid assistant vacancy and what training it pays for; I won't leave my current wage without an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with some energy to learn. I do not expect a course alone to protect our house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you practise with the trainer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show my trainer the two claims I misunderstood and ask her to walk me through the correction. That is a better lesson than racing through a screen by myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make care work possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The care home would need to offer paid hours that cover my share of the mortgage. I would ask how much practical training happens on the clock before putting in an application.

Learn which **AI suggestions fail** by logging errors from assigned cases.

feel: **Anxious**, though supervised practice gives me something useful to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say general AI by 2028 could answer our calls before most of us finish learning the harder ones. Robots around 2031 come later, but they do not protect a call-centre shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my junior role might end quickly. My husband's school-maintenance pay does not cover our mortgage, food and two children alone, and our reserve is under a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'll ask my manager for a written notice date and ask the care home about any paid assistant opening with supervised shifts. If my centre job ends in the first year after 2028, I'll apply for a posted care vacancy only if its hours and wages cover our bills, and ask my mother to watch the children during interviews only if she is free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can make calls, but two years is short when our savings are almost empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change at home first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my husband we need to keep the mortgage payment first and cut the weekend outings if my pay stops. I would tell the children only what changes for them, not promise a job I do not have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can your mother cover interview days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother already helps another family member some afternoons. I would ask her which interview days she can actually cover rather than assume she can take the children whenever I need.

I'd tell agents **2031 robots** do not extend our headset jobs.
think: I expect my **junior role** could end soon.
I know my husband's **maintenance wage** cannot cover all four of us alone.
do: Request a **written notice date** from my manager now.
Apply for **posted paid care work** after a real cut only if wages and hours cover bills.
Ask my **mother about interview childcare** only when she is free.
feel: **Alarmed** by a short clock and less than one month saved.
S2.quote: My husband's school-maintenance pay does not cover our mortgage, food and two children alone, and our reserve is under a month.
fieldNote: The **husband's wage** is insufficient for the whole household.
She treats **care work** as a paid opening, not a guaranteed refuge from later robots.
Her mother's **childcare help** is conditional on available time.

steps.text: Apply for posted paid care work after a cut only if wages and hours cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for the centre to give us paid training dates and honest staffing numbers. Our calls face full AGI in 2031, before hands-on robots arrive around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could finish learning claims and also see whether I can do care work well. I know robots may reach the hands-on part later, so I would not call it a job for life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll practise claims on paid shifts and ask the care home about a supervised paid trial day. If it posts a paid assistant role with hours and wages that cover our bills, I'll try the day and apply before 2031; in the first year after AGI, I'll keep whichever real wage we have while I check openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not trapped. Five years gives me time to see a full workday before changing fields.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see on the trial day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to see lifting, cleaning and a difficult conversation, not just the friendly part of a visit. If the trial is unpaid, I would stay at the centre and ask again later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who covers the children for the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask my husband to cover the children for the trial day only if his school shift allows it. We cannot lose two wages to test one job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives us time to build skills while we still receive wages. General AI reaches calls in 2036, while hands-on robots arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 my children may still need help, and our mortgage may remain; I won't assume either burden is gone. I could become reliable at claims or learn a care job if the paid opening exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll keep my call shift, practise claims with the trainer and put any extra pay toward the mortgage reserve. If AGI arrives in 2036, I'll apply in its first year for a posted paid care role only if my hours fall and the new wage covers our bills; otherwise I'll keep my centre job while it pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, though there is room to think. A decade does not pay this month's mortgage, but it gives me time to practise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask my children what work they enjoy as they grow, not tell them to follow my fears. Their choices should not be set by a prediction about my desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for care training now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not take a care course from our savings now. If the care home offered paid training tied to a real job later, I would consider it after checking the wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. I could lose the junior desk before I learn the hard claims, and we have almost no reserve for the mortgage. Written notice, a paid care opening with enough hours and training on the clock would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how a junior agent is supposed to practise when the simple calls vanish. A real caller's bill is not a safe place for my first try at a new system. We need supervised time before the difficult calls are all that's left.

headlineQuote: A real caller's bill is not a safe place for my first try at a new system.
portrait: Lena is a **43-year-old junior agent** at a contact centre, with secondary schooling and difficult claims still to learn.
Her **low pay** and savings below one month sit beside a mortgage, two schoolchildren and her husband's maintenance wage.
She uses **AI occasionally** after experienced agents prove it works, and asks for supervised practice on paid shifts.
The **2028 date** alarms her; a longer runway lets her test paid care work without treating later robots as harmless.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase her junior desk before she builds skill or a mortgage buffer.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice** would tell her when to seek another paid role.
A **care vacancy** with enough hours and paid training would give her a practical route.
